demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He is an environmental scientist, seventy-eight years old, and he has not driven since the accident. That is the first thing he tells me, not as a confession, but as a fact—a piece of himself he has learned to accept. The accident happened two years ago, on a gravel road in the desert, where he was collecting soil samples for a long-term contamination study. He had done the same route for decades. That morning, the sun was low, and he was alone in his pickup, thinking about a conversation with his wife. He does not remember seeing the young field assistant. He only remembers the thud, the jolt of the truck, and his own voice shouting something in his native language that he could not later translate.

The assistant was a twenty-two-year-old intern who had wandered ahead of the group. He was walking along the shoulder, listening to music, and he stepped into the road just as the sun blinded him. The impact shattered his femur and crushed his pelvis. He nearly died. The man survived, after multiple surgeries, but he will always walk with a limp, and he will never run again. The scientist visited him once in the hospital. The intern’s mother was there, crying, and she did not look at him. He has not spoken to the intern since. He cannot bring himself to call, though he has the number. He tells me he can still feel the weight of the steering wheel in his hands, the way the truck slid on loose gravel, the smell of dust and antifreeze.

Now he works exclusively from home, analyzing satellite imagery and writing environmental impact reports. He avoids fieldwork entirely. His colleagues do not understand why he turned down a major project last spring—a wetland survey he had spent his entire career hoping to lead. They think he is old, tired, finally ready to slow down. He lets them think that. The truth is, he cannot be near a vehicle on unpaved roads. He cannot be around young researchers who laugh and walk too close to the path. He cannot concentrate on the data because his mind keeps replaying the split second before the impact: the glare, the movement in his peripheral vision, the impossible pause before everything changed.

His wife cooks for him, talks to him, tries to draw him into conversation about their grandchildren. He listens but does not respond. He does not want her to worry, so he pretends to read the newspaper, but the letters blur and he sees only that day. At night, he wakes to the sound of his own voice calling out. He does not tell her what he dreams about. Once, he tried to explain the guilt—how it sits inside him like a stone—but she said, “It was an accident. You are not a bad man.” He knows she is right, but knowing does not change the feeling. He no longer looks in the mirror when he shaves. He no longer takes walks after dinner, because the streetlights remind him of the headlights.

He has started attending a small mosque occasionally, but he cannot bring himself to pray. He feels unworthy. He thinks the imam would see what he did, even though he knows it is not a sin, just a mistake. He avoids the news. He avoids the television. When his daughter calls, he finds reasons to hang up quickly. He does not know how to tell her that he is afraid of himself now—afraid that he could hurt someone else without meaning to, afraid that his own hands are not safe.

The soil reports pile up on his desk. He stares at them for hours, but he has not sent a completed analysis in six months. His supervisor has started asking gentle questions. He does not know how long he can keep pretending everything is fine.
